In the Railway Committee, the matter was brought to the attention of the Minister of Railways and of the Chairman as to the powers given to this railway to operate a commercial telephone line. I am advised that in the past in Bills of this character, such powers have not been granted to railroads. In the province of Alberta we have a government-owned telephone system operating throughout the province, and operating in sections where there are no railroads. We are not anxious that any railroad or other company shall be given federal powers to operate a commercial telephone line. If the powers were limited simply to the use of the telephone service by the railroad on its own system for its own purposes, the matter would be different; but as I understand it, this company are asking for powers to operate a telephone system along their line of railroad and also to do a commercial business. In our provincial charters no powers of this character are granted. The Prime Minister of the province of Alberta informs me that in the past such powers have not been given to railroads. The explanation given in the committee the other day was not quite clear to me, and I would be glad if the minister would make a statement in regard to this clause.

I received a letter from the Prime Minister, Mr. Sifton, on this very point, and I had the matter looked into. I find that every year powers are granted similar to those in this clause.
On section 8-railway authorized:

When this Bill was up in the Railway Committee on Friday, it was

pointed out, by mention of the principal points, that the route of 'the proposed railroad between Winnipeg and Edmonton, closely paralleled the Canadian Pacific railway, which also parallels the Grand Trunk railway and the Canadian Northern railway. The question was raised as to what "the policy of the Government was in such a case. Some statement was made to the effect that the 'minister in committee had stated that, should the railway company undertake to build and come to him for approval of its plans, he would not approve of plans that would allow the line to pass within some certain distance of the lines already existing, except where it passed through important points. I am sure the committee would be glad if the minister would make a statement as to the policy of the Government with regard to that rather important matter.

I do not think I made a statement in the committee, but the solicitor acting on behalf of this company made that statement, that the policy of the department in approving of locations was that, except at central points where the railways had to come in, they would have to keep twenty 'miles apart. I think I explained to the House a year ago that I had adopted a policy that on branch lines-of course this may be considered a trunk line-we would insist on their being twenty miles apart. If this is considered as a trunk line, then of course it would be dealt with in the same manner as the three great transcontinental roads, that is, it would have the right to the shortest route. If it is considered as a branch line, it would come under the branch line policy.

I merely want to know
what the policy of the Government is. The hon. minister quotes what a solicitor of the railway company has said. What we are anxious to have is a statement of the Government treating this railway as a trunk line, which it is.

If it is a trunk line,
the company will get the same consideration as the others and will not be dealt with under our policy as to branch lines.

That is, they would be
entitled to the shortest line between important points ?
Yes.

In other words, they
might parallel already existing lines?
Yes.

No doubt circumstances
sometimes occur that render it right and proper that railway lines should parallel each other, but I think that the Government would be well advised to take into consideration the conditions of the western country before being committed to the declaration as my hon. friend has made it. There are three trunk lines already in existence between Winnipeg and Edmonton at varying distances from each other. At Saskatoon the three are within a distance of sixteen miles.
For a very large part of the distance two, and in some cases three of the lines are comparatively close together. The building of a fourth line along that route means a vast expenditure of capital, and such a line, in order to compete, would have to be built according to the very highest standard or it would not compete at all. It is a matter of very great doubt whether the Government is wise in committing itself to this policy, when we consider the vast areas in the prairie provinces that still remain absolutely without railway communication, where people are 70, 80 or 90 miles from a railroad. Capital must be found to give the railway accommodation that will benefit these settlers, and render possible the development of the country. Where there is such a great need for 'capital for railroad construction, in order that present settlers may be accommodated and the proper development of the country obtained, I say that the Government should be very cautious about sanctioning a project of unnecessary duplication. I am strongly in favour of railroad competition. As I have pointed out, throughout a great part of the distance between Winnipeg and Edmonton three railways are now in active competition. It seems to me that these ought to afford measurably sufficient accommodation for that section of the country, and that those sections which are suffering serious hardships because of the lack of railway communication, and where the country at large is subject to the direct loss resulting from the lack of development that would accrue from railroad construction, should be given consideration. It seems to me to be a doubtful policy on the part of the Government to sanction this fourth line simply as a competing line when competition already exists, and when there is so much need for railway communication in other directions.

I suppose it is useless to try to get the minister to say anything further on this subject. This Bill was held over, I understand, for consideration in the presence of the minister, and in order that he might have an opportunity of giving his opinion on certain matters which have just been brought before the committee by the hon. member for Edmonton. The minister tells us that the solicitor for this company stated what the policy of the company would be. That is surely very useful information; the solicitor surely speaks with a great deal of authority. When he comes before the Railway Committee he may tell the members of the committee practically anything that comes into his head. He is not responsible for carrying the project out, and the company he represents are not bound by any assertions he may make. Here is a line that practically parallels the present line of the Canadian Pacific railway; that is, the Manitoba and North Western line, and its extension. If this company goes ahead and finances this proposition, and if they come down here to have their plans approved by the minister, will he sanction plans permitting the construction of a road paralleling, within half a mile or a mile, the Canadian Pacific railway, from Winnipeg right through to Edmonton, a distance of over 800 miles, when there is such an enormous demand for railroad communication and transportation facilities in many other portions of western Canada? That is what we want to know; I wish the minister would talk and tell us what his policy is. Never having visited Egypt, I have not had the privilege of looking at the Sphynx, which, it is said, although made of stone, looks very wise. The minister may have a splendid policy in his mind, but we would like to know whether his seeming wisdom is real, or whether it is of a character similar to that massive work of art which may be found in that ancient country known as Egypt. If the minister will state frankly whether he will or not permit the construction of this line paralleling the Canadian Pacific railway from Winnipeg to Edmonton, then we will know whether the country is to be served by this enormous expenditure of capital. We want competition, but not the kind of competition that spells ruin to the railways and no benefit to the people. We want competition that will mean transportation facilities for the people who have not the 
benefit of such facilities now. Does the minister propose 'to put that policy into effect, or does he not?

I cannot help observing the change that has come over the hon. gentlemen of the Opposition during the last two or three years. It is only two or three years since hon. gentlemen on the opposite side of the House had a good deal more to do with the legislation that passes through the House than they have at the present time. I have listened for hours in the Railway Committee, and sometimes in the House, to some of the hon. gentlemen who have spoken on the other side against granting this charter. These gentlemen urged at that time free trade in charters-let everybody come along and get a charter. But a change has come over the attitude taken by hon. gentlemen in thi3 respect-I do not know just- why. The hon. member who has just taken his seat spoke about the need of competition. The gentlemen asking for this charter are not, I understand, one of the great corporations that already have a line right through to Edmonton, and if the charter were granted the hon. gentleman might naturally expect that there would. be some competition. I cannot see any good reason why 'a Bill of this kind should not be passed by the committee, and why these men should not be given a chance to build this road if they want to. Four or five years ago the policy urged very strongly by hon. gentlemen opposite was that any man who asked for a charter should be given one. These people are not asking for a subsidy.

We are not opposing this
charter.

I understood from
the remarks of the hon. gentleman that he was opposing it. Bo far as paralleling the lines is concerned, I am not sure that hon. gentlemen opposite have always adhered very strictly to the doctrines which they now put forward. In connection with-the construction of the Transcontinental, it was contended very strongly by hon. gentlemen now on this side of the House that the route on the Transcontinental west of Winnipeg was not going to serve the country in the manner which was intended when the charter was first brought before this House. It was intended to run farther north, but it was brought down south, going around the bottom of lake Manitoba, and, as every-

body knows, it parallels the Canadian Pacific railway and the Canadian Northern railway. I believe that the gentlemen who are asking for this charter are asking for it in good faith. There is a Large territory lying north of those lines not now served by any railway.
Let them go north.

They could go north
and may go north, but I cannot see any good reason for the opposition given to the Bill. I think the Bill should go through and that we should give these gentlemen an opportunity of constructing this road if they want to.

I thought I had made myself clear to the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver). I said that if this _ was a trunk line I should not interfere, that they would be entitled, like all trunk lines, to get the shortest and best line they could; but that if it was a branch line, 1 had laid down a policy in my department a year ago that I would not approve of lines within twenty miles of one another. I have heard that this is an extension of a line that is being built into the Peace river now and the promoters want to get an outlet. That I am not sure of, it is all hearsay. As to my not saying much, 1 often think if a lot of people said less they would get on better.
_>Ir. OLIVER:	It makes very little difference whether or not this charter, or in fact almost any other charter, is granted if no subsidy or Government assistance goes with it. Free trade in charters is practically all right, although I do not see why there is a Railway Committee at all, or why the time of this House is taken up in discussing railway charters, if there is to be absolute free trade in them. However, it makes no difference whether charters such as this are granted by Parliament, the question is as to the granting of aid. It is not the approval of plans upon which we - are so anxious to have the Government's policy.

No subsidy is being
asked for.

My hon. friend knows
perfectly well that this road will not be built without a Government subsidy or assistance of some kind.

That will be time
enough to discuss it.

I think we are entitled
to know now what the policy of the Government is or will be in regard to a charter absolutely paralleling three other lines.
Mr. SAM. HUGHES: How far apart will the two lines be?

Touching Yorkton and
Saskatoon 1#ie road, if it is at all a straight one, must necessarily parallel the Canadian Pacific railway within a very few miles in part of its course and in many places it must parallel the Grand Trunk or the Canadian Northern railway. It would not parallel the three within a few miles but throughout its course it must parallel two of them. I think it would be fair and right that the Government should declare here and now whether their policy is and will be to grant assistance to a new line built under such conditions. I ask this for the reasons I placed before the House a few minutes ago-the urgent requirements in many sections of the country which are at present without railroad communication. I think that makes it reasonable that we should ask for an announcement of the policy of the Government in regard to this road. I said that I knew a settlement 90 miles from the railroad. I was very far within the mark. I have in mind a settlement now of sixteen townships in which nearly every acre is under homestead or bounty warrant entries. It is 250 miles from the nearest possible railway point. That is at Grand Prairie, Peace river.

There are roads
building in there at the present time.

There is a road being
built in there, but it is being built at such a rate that it will be a number of years before it gets there and it is not being built on any aid or assistance from this Parliament, it is being built on provincial aid. There is not only this Grand Prairie settlement in the Peace river country but there are other settled sections of the Peace river that are from 230 to 350 miles from railroads. These people have gone in there expecting railroad communication. It is true that the provincial government is trying to meet the case, but it seems to me to be a duty which lies On the Dominion Government to meet the case rather than the provincial; and when demands are being made or are in prospect for aid for 800 miles of line that will absolutely parallel three other lines, we would like to know what the position of the Government is in regard to aiding such a line when aid is so

greatly needed for other lines in other sections of the country where there is not only no competition but no railroad communication at all.

I do not think any
fixed policy should be laid down as to what roads should get aid and what should not. The facts of the whole case shqpld be put before the Government and before the House even, before we could lay down any rule. I endorse what the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) said on the other Bill, that applications of this kind should be treated on their merits as they come. From the case the hon. member makes out of the line building in there now, I think that is a road that should be aided. I believe in opening and developing the country, and I would say that if aid is being given to any road this seems one that should receive assistance. I do not know whether this road is going to be a trunk line or not. If it was up for approval of plans I would know something about it, 1 could ask questions; but the promoters are not here, and I do not want to prejudge their case.	[DOT]
On the preamble:

Does section 10 authorize the company to establish telephone lines and do a telephone business throughout, the country at large, or can the company build only along the line of railway? There can be no objection to the company doing this latter.

The clause has always been inserted. It is pretty clear:
The company may, subject to the provisions of the Railway Act, construct and operate telegraph and telephone lines upon its railway and establish offices for and undertake the transmission of messages for the public and collect tolls therefor, etc.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It seems to restrict the operation to the railway line.

I think it is pretty well covered by the first two lines, ' subject to the Railway Act.' I would just like to say a word in reference to free trade in charters. It might be that what we call free trade in charters was all right a few years ago, but is not all right now. We cannot lay down an absolute rule for all time. Where there are no transportation facilities, I have always maintained that any company applying for a charter should have it, but it is a little different where there are already several lines of railway. Too many lines of railway are almost as serious as not having enough.
(Mr. Oliver.]
Where capital is locked up in three or four lines covering the same territory, I am not sure that competition is very keen. Either the railways must lose money, or their patrons are helping to pay dividends on three railways instead of on one. So long as the Board of Railway Commissioners has the right to control rates, that largely overcomes the objection to no competition, but there is this other point: in discussing the decision as to rates in the West, hon. members will have noticed in the press certain references to the effect that if rates were reduced beyond a certain point, some companies might be .able to stand it, and other companies might not be able to stand it. You might give a charter to a weak company to build 700 to 800 miles of railway where already three lines are operating, and then the argument could be put up a little later on, you cannot reduce the freight rates because while the three large companies can stand it, the poor company cannot.

Would you refuse
them a charter?

I do not know that I would. I would put them far enough apart. It is a difficult question to disduss, and it is hard to lay down a rule from which you cannot deviate. I see no reason why this company should not receive its charter if it is a sufficient distance away from the other line to get enough traffic to support it, but if it go very close to the other lines it is questionable whether it ought to be allowed to lock up that much more money. Instead of being a factor in reducing rates, it might be an argument for keeping rates up.

Preamble agreed to.

1.	Is the Minister of Agriculture aware of certain statements which the newspaper Le Devoir mentions in its issue of the 5th of February, 1914, as having been made by the Hon. Mr. Caron, Minister of Agriculture in the Quebec Government at a sitting of that Legislature, and which is as follows:
'If the minister does not go too far, a great many of the dairy herds are affected with tuberculosis, and it is the same with half of the pork we eat. That is what Mr. Caron has stated twice. And he, Mr. Caron, has even added that it would not surprise him sliouid the medical corps come to the conclusion that the cause of tuberculosis affecting human beings is mostly to be found there.
Mr. Caron holds the federal Government responsible for that because it refused to appropriate a part of the special grant intended for agricultural purposes to inspecting the herds. Ottawa told us, says the minister, that it was so important a matter that it would itself deal with it. That delighted me, further said Mr. Caron but Ottawa has done nothing so far'.
That most serious statement was uttered during a debate on the federal subsidy towards agriculture. The minister unceasingly complains that the conditions of the grant prevent him from following a definite programme; that

there is a discrimination between the way of dealing with the province of Quebec and the others, because it has not been, at first, consulted, and in the second place, because a guardian is imposed upon it to supervise the spending of the moneys in question. Know you that under and by virtue of Part 11 of the Inquiries Act, chapter 104, Revised Statutes, 1906, and under the authority of an order of His Excellency, the Administrator of the Government of Canada in Council made in pursuance of said part 11 and bearing date the twenty-fifth day of August, in the year of Oui Lord one thousand nine hundred and thirteen (a copy of which is hereto annexed), and by virtue of all and every other power in that behalf vested in me, I the Honourable Charles Doherty, Minister of Justice of Canada, do hereby nominate, constitute and appoint you, the said George Milnes Macdonnell, you the said Frederick Ether-ington, and you the said Joseph Patrick Downey, to be commissioners to investigate and report upon the following matters:
(a)	The state and management of Kingston penitentiary.
(b)	The conduct of the officers and employees of said penitentiary so far as the same relates to their official duties, and
(c)	Generally the subject of the conduct and administration of penitentiaries, including such methods as may conduce to the permanent reformation of the convicts and, without prejudice to the punishment which convicts should properly undergo and without undue burden upon the public funds, tend to mitigate as far as may be found possible the sufferings entailed by their confinement upon those dependent upon them.
Provided that the inquiries under which paragraphs (a) and (b) shall not extend back over a longer period than five years, except in so far as the commissioners may deem it desirable in the public interest to inquire into any particular matters antecedent to such period.
And we do further nominate, constitute and appoint you, the said George Milnes Macdonnell to be chairman of the said commission.
To have, hold, exercise and enjoy the office of commissioners as aforesaid unto you the said George Milnes Macdonnell, you file said. Frederick Etherington, and

you the said Joseph Patrick Downey, together with all and every the powers, rights, authority, privileges, emoluments and advantages by virtue of said part 11 and otherwise unto the said office of right and by law appertaining.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. B. NORTHRUP (East Hastings) moved:
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the procedure under which divorces are granted by Parliament and the consequent unreasonable expense thereof are so unsatisfactory, besides being prohibitive to tr>e great maioritv of the people of Canada, that the same should be taken into immediate consideration by the Government with a view to reform, during the present session.
He said: In connection with the subject of divorce, there are two separate and distinct questions which might engage the attention of the House. On the one hand, this House might be asked by an Act to extend the grounds on which divorce may be granted. The most careless perusal of this resolution will show that it has no reference whatever to anything of that kind. There is another course that might be taken by this House in connection with
divorce, and that is to consider whether or not the procedure under which divorces are granted is the most satisfactory procedure to all classes of the community, and the least expensive to those who can least afford to bear that expense. We all know that in our Dominion four provinces, namely, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and British Columbia, have jurisdiction over divorce. In the other five provinces, Saskatchewan, Alberta, Manitoba, Ontario, and Quebec, the courts have not jurisdiction; so that for the whole Dominion, other than the first named four provinces, any divorces that have been granted in this country since Confederation have been granted by this House.
It being conceded, as the fact certainly is, that divorces are granted by Parliament, it must also be conceded that they are granted either as a right or as a favour. If divorces are granted by this Parliament as a right, then certainly every man in this country should have an equal right to secure a divorce. If, on the other hand,- and I hardly imagine that any one would maintain this-divorces by this Parliament are to be granted as a favour, then certainly they should be granted to those who need the favour most, instead of, as at present, to those who need it the least. One has only to consider the experience of every one in this House to come to a speedy conclusion as to whether or not our present procedure is satisfactory. I will deal with that later on, but in the meantime I would like to point out that of all the civilized countries in the world there is but one that rivals us m our procedure, and that is poor old Ireland. Most of us have some suspicion, from items we have occasionally seen in the newspapers of late, that there is a little difference of opinion as to how Ireland should be governed in the future; but I venture to say there is no difference of opinion whatever, anywhere in the civilized world, as to whether or not Ireland has been the model government with the wisest legislation for 800 or 900 years. And yet Ireland is the only country which at all approaches our method of granting divorces.
To really understand the position we occupy and-if 1 may be pardoned for saying it-the utterly absurd and grotesque procedure we have, perhaps it may not be out ol place to remind the House of the procedure in other countries, and in other times. Up to the time of the Reformation, it is well known, there was no such thing as divorce in the western church as we understand divorce to-day. We read of

divorces being granted, a mensa et thoro, or, as we would say, a judicial separation without any right given to the parties to marry again. There was also introduced into the western church the right to have marriages, that had been validly celebrated, set aside on the ground of nullity.
I do not intend to occupy any time in discussing that question; but merely in order that we may understand what the practice has been, I will call the attention of the House to the important evidence given by Monseigneur Moyes before the Royal Commission on Divorce and Matrimonial Causes, vol. 2, page 426. Monseigneur Moyes saying that he was a canon of the archdiocese of Westminster, a prelate of the Roman Court, and that he had attended on behalf of the Catholic Church at the request of the Archbishop of Westminster. I think I can hardly be said to introduce anything contentious when, merely to give the historical reasons for it, 1 point out that prior to the Reformation and up to the present time, while divorce in our sense is absolutely unknown, there are a number of grounds, fifteen in all, on which marriages are liable to be declared null and void. Mgr. Moyes in his evidence says:
The impediments which are held by the Catholic church to be diriment or nullifying are the following:	1. Error, as to person. 2. Condition (if A marries B, a slave, believing B to be free). 3. Solemn vow of chastity or entering religious order, made before consummation of marriage. 4. Consanguinity to third degree. 5. Crime (if A during a former marriage with B has committed adultery with C, witli promise of marriage after death of B, and if A or C has attempted the life of B, the marriage of A and C is null). 6. Disparity of worship, viz., marriage of a Christian with a non-Christian. 7. Duress or violence affecting liberty of consort. 8 Holy order to which is attached obligation of chastity. 9. The bond of preceding marriage (if either party have a husband or wife still alive). 10. Public decorum (if one of the parties is solemnly or publicly betrothed to another person). 11. Madness or amentia (viz, imbecility precluding reasonable consent). 12. Affinity. 13. Clandestinity. 14. Impoteney. 15. Rape.
So that we find that in the Western Church, up to the time of the Reformation, while there were no divorces a vinculo matrimonii, there were fifteen different grounds upon which the ecclesiastical courts did declare marriages to be null and void. If there were children as a result of these marriages, inasmuch as the marriages were liable to be declared null and void, the ine"itable result was the bastardizing of the children.
I Mr. Northrup.]
In the Eastern Church, which was the Greek church, divorce was always allowed. Prior to the Reformation the church court had claimed the right to deal exclusively with matrimonial causes, and the state throughout western Europe allowed this claim, so that all causes having to do with matrimonial disputes were tried before the ecclesiastical courts. After the Reformation in England it became impossible that the old procedure or trial in ecclesiastical courts should be continued, and there was no procedure open to the people of England in order to obtain divorce. After a time it was seen that Parliament might deal with this question, as with any other subject, and it became the custom in England, and continued until the Matrimonial Causes Act of 1857 was passed, that divorces could be obtained by Act of Parliament. Subsequently rules were passed by which it was necessary, first, to obtain a divorce a mensa et thoro, a judicial separation from the offending partner, and then to issue a writ and obtain a verdict for damages against the co-respondent, or to satisfy Parliament that there were good and sufficient reasons why that course had not been taken. At last, in 1857, it became evident that the course of procedure up to that time was unsatisfactory. Many attempts had been made to change that course, but although practically everybody agreed that the course -was absurd and abominably expensive, yet, with that English unreadiness to move, it was as hard to cause a change in the law in that respect as it was to cause, a change in the law under which people were hanged for over one hundred various offences. At last Mr. Justice Maule gave his famous sentence for bigamy at Warwick, which, having convulsed the nation, led to the law as they have it in England to-day. I will take the liberty of reading this sentence pronounced by Mr. Justice Maule, inasmuch as it had such a tremendous effect upon the public sentiment of England.
What year?
1845, I think.
What is the case.

A man had been convicted of bigamy, and this was the sentence pronounced by the judge upon the prisoner:
Prisoner, you have been convicted upon clear evidence; you have intermarried with another woman, your lawful wife being still alive. you have committed the crime of bigamy. you tell

out, for I remember a divorce not very long ago passed by this Parliament without the shadow or tittle of evidence of adultery- but theoretically the assumption is that divorce can only be granted by this Parliament on the ground of adultery. Still, being a matter of legislation in Canada, if a writer were describing the grounds on which divorce could be granted by this Parliament, he would have to admit that, whatever we might do practically, however we may find ourselves bound by the rules in that respect, legally and constitutionally we can grant a divorce on any grounds, no matter how trifling. That, in itself, I submit, is rather an objectionable feature.
In the province of Ontario, and I believe in all the provinces, if the husband has suddenly disappeared and has not been heard of for seven years, there is a legal presumption of death. After seven years, his wife, or children if he has not a wife, can apply to the courts and they divide the property he left among those who would be entitled to it in case he was actually dead. If his w'ife, relying on that presumption of death, and having obtained her share of the property as his widow, should see fit to marry again, originally she would be liable to bigamy if the husband turned up, no matter how honestly she may have believed that he had been dead. Seeing the utter absurdity and injustice of that, our Criminal Code has been amended, so that now, after seven years' absence of the husband, the wife, having good reason to think the husband dead, if she should marry again, would not be liable under the Criminal Code for bigamy. But see the position the unfortunate woman is placed in. It is said here that the judge will take judicial notice of the husband's death, and will divide his property, and that his wife can marry again, and be perfectly free from any penalty under the criminal law; but yet if the husband should turn up, or if evidence should be given to show that he had been alive after her second marriage, we would condemn that poor woman to the -shame of being the mistress of the man who she thought was her husband. And what have you done to her unfortunate children, if there are any, of the marriage? Speaking as Canadians, and claiming to be among the freest and greatest liberty-loving people in the world, can any Canadian say, that is right? If a woman such as that in good faith marries again, after the courts of the land have said her husband was dead, can -any man in this House say that it is fair that she should be treated as the mistress 
of the man whom she married, and that her unfortunate children, born within the second marriage, -should be bastardized by the law of the land?
I heard of a case recently from the province of British Columbia, which illustrates one of the absurdities of our law. A lady married a man who was the manager of a bank; she lived with him as his wife, and they had three children. He induced her father, who was a wealthy man, to endorse [DOT]for him, and one day he disappeared apparently from the face of the earth. He was -away for seven years, and then the lady consulted a lawyer in British Columbia to ask him if she could have a divorce. He was obliged to advise her that she could not. In British Columbia they have a divorce court, and, so far 'as the expense went, s'he might have applied there. Here we have judicial proceedings, and she might have applied here, but the difficulty was that the man had simply disappeared, -and there was no evidence that he was dead. A friend suspecting that the man might have returned to the place in England whence he came, spent some money engaging detectives to trace him, and they found he was living in England with another woman whom he represented to be his wife. What could be done in British Columbia for the unfortunate legal wife? Under the laws of British Columbia she could only obtain a divorce on certain grounds, such .as were provided in England under the original 1857 Act. Under that Ac-t the husband could obtain a divorce on the ground of adultery alone, but the wife could not obtain a divorce unless there was adultery coupled with cruelty. That was the law introduced in the province of British Columbia. Some years later, owing to the hardships that arose in England from that law, an amendment was brought in so that desertion for two years would take the place of cruelty,. and if the adultery could be proved, together with desertion for two years, the unfortunate woman could obtain relief. But that did not apply in British Columbia. Therefore, the position of this woman was, that although she could get the evidence to show that her husband was living in England with another woman, she could not apply before the courts of British Columbia because she had not the proof of cruelty to help her out. And she could not come to this Parliament, because a poor woman with three children, [DOT] earning her own living, and supporting her children in British Columbia, was not in a position to file a petition

with this House; to pay detectives in the old country, to bring them out here to prove her case, and go to the expense that would bd necessary to satisfy a committee of t(hi s Parliament that she was entitled to a divorce. There are many cases such as that.
I have had, in my own experience, cases which show the injustice of the present procedure. One man from my own part of the country came to me saying that his wife had eloped with another man and was living with him in a town in the United States, and he asked me what he could do.
' I had to tell him frankly that the only thing I could see for him to do was to get rich, in the first place, because this country did not recognize any right on the part of a poor man to have a divorce. This unfortunate husband was left with four or five little children, from eight to twelve ytears of age, and what possible justification could there be for imposing the penalty we do impose on these little children, by practically forbidding the father to obtain a divorce. In circumstances such as these, with a man earning a couple of dollars a day and living in a little house, it is perfectly evident that he cannot afford to hire a housekeeper to look after his house and his children. If he does bring in a woman for that purpose, the latter end may be worse than the first. On the other hand, if he does not do so, these little children, left to grow up without a mother's protecting care, stand a bad chance in the world.
I think the members of this House will appreciate the fact that we have a duty to perform. We are really trustees for the people; and if we allow a state of affairs to continue which is felt to be an injustice by any portion of the people, we are contrib-ut.ng something to increase the unfortunate unrest which at present is so rife throughout the whole world. It is idle to ignore the fact that the world has never been so beset by perplexing problems as it is at the present time, and among them the social and the industrial problems are perhaps among the greatest and most perplexing.
Putting the case on no other ground, leaving out of sight for the moment the uniortunate victim of an unhappy matrimonial alliance, leaving out of sight the little children who are certainly in no way to blame, but who must to a certain extent pay the penalty, looking at the question from the standpoint of the state, is it in the interest of a young country like Canada, with a population rapidly increasing by
outsiders coming in from other lands, that a feeling of dissatisfaction, of injustice should pervade the minds of a large portion of the people who feel that others can have what they cannot have? I believe that it would really be better and fairer either to forbid all divorces or to make the procedure such that all would be able to obtain advantage of what, as I said a few moment-ago, is either a right or a favour.
If a man or a woman desires a divorce from this Parliament, the first step is to advertise for six months in the Canada Gazette. Can anybody imagine anything more absolutely absurd than that? What conceivable benefit is to be derived by advertising for six months in the- Canada Gazette? Of course, a divorce Bill is a Private Bill, and in the majority of Private Bills for charters of railway companies and corporations, one can quite understand how it would be proper that notice be given to all parties interested. In a divorce case, inasmuch as you have to serve the party interested with a notice of procedure, and the man or woman who has run away with somebody else is not very apt to while away the long hours of a dreary winter in another land by reading the Canada Gazette, that seems an absurd step.
The party has then to advertise in two papers in the county in which he or she resides. Again I ask for what purpose?
The proceedings here are so ex-9 p.m. pensive-$210 is the first item to be paid-that a poor person practically cannot obtain a divorce.
Then there is another matter that is known to every hon. member. Could there possibly be a greater scandal, could there by anything more calculated to bring our proceedings and ourselves under contempt, than the amount of lobbying that every member knows goes on in connection with divorce Bills? Is it not a fact that the senators and the members of this House are beset by those who are interested in the decisions to be given under divorce petitions? Only last session-and this perhaps brought the question to my mind more closely than it had been brought before-I happened, in room 16, to speak of a certain divorce which was before the House. I spoke rather unfavourably as to the prospects of one party to the divorce. When I arrived home on the following Sunday, I found that the fair petitioner was in my parlour to interview me. We are supposed to be sitting here as judges. Can one conceive of a state of judicial procedure in

which it is considered the proper thing for the litigant, particularly if she is young and pretty, to intercede for justice with the judge between the sitttings of the court?
After the petition is brought into the Senate, it is referred to a committee of nine members, three of whom are lawyers. While the procedure, as I have said before, is most absurd and grotesque, I think it is only fair to say a word in commendation of the Chairman who for so many years has so faithfully, so energetically and so well presided over the Senate Committee. I believe that Senator Kirchhoffer, who this session has been obliged, through what I hope is only temporary indisposition, to allow another gentleman to take his place, has presided over the committee for seventeen years. During that period I believe that *only one Bill, that came from the Senate Committee to the Senate, eventually did not pass, and I believe that one Bill that come to this House last session did not pass.
The work of that committee has been onerous even if it has been rather absurd. We all know that the Senate has frequent and lengthy adjournments. A divorce petition is set down for hearing, and when the witnesses arrive from Winnipeg, Vancouver or Halifax-not from Halifax, because Nova Scotia has a divorce court of its own-it is found that the Senate has adjourned and will not sit for a couple of weeks. Then the Chairman has to hunt around and get a quorum to save the people the extra expense that might be incurred. Thus the committee has to sit not only while the House is in session, but while the House is adjourned, in order to carry on its business. If it had not been for the care, the wise legal ability of the Chairman of the Senate, the abuses that would naturally flow, and that to a certain extent have flowed from our system, would have become so intolerable long ago that the present state of the law would have been entirely changed.
I do not desire to occupy the time of the House longer, because it is not my object to lay down a remedy. I am asking the Government of the day, asking the House, asking any members who take an interest in this most important question, to endeavour to solve a difficulty which certainly exists at the present time. Perhaps I may be laughed at for saying this, but it seems to me that, if I am right in the views that I have expressed, this is a subject which members on both sides of the House might fairly and honestly discuss and for which they might try to work out a remedy that not only would be just to many of our 
fellow citizens, but would save a great many heart burnings through those feeings of injustice which certainly exist at the present time. I hope the Government will take the matter into consideration. If the Government and the House are perfectly satisfied that the present system of procedure is the best that can be devised, and that in no way can a simpler or cheaper procedure be discovered, then by all means let us cling .to our present procedure. But if there is any way in which the procedure can be simplified and the expense lessened, I beg of the Government and of the House to do their best to attain that end.
In conclusion, I would like to say that in the line which I am taking in this case, I am following exactly the line taken by one of the commissioners appointed under this Royal Commission in 1910-' our trusty and entirely beloved counsellor Cosmo Gordon, Archbishop of York, Primate of England and Meropolitan.' When I take the view expressed by the Archbishop of York, the Primate of England, I at all events cannot be accused of trying to stir up strife. On the contrary, I am trying to obtain justice if possible. Let me point out-because the matter may be referred to later on and may not be represented as it should b*- that this Matrimonal Causes Commission was appointed in 1909, and I am sure it would be instructive to look for a moment at ^ some of the reasons why it was appointed. I read the following frem the warrant of their appointment:
Whereas we have deemed it expedient that a commission should forthwith issue to inquire into the present state of the law and the ad-mmstration thereof in divorce or matrimonial causes and applications for separation orders, especially with regard to the position of the poorer classes in relation thereto.
Then it goes on:
And we do hereby empower you to make an interim report with a view to making such suggestions as you may recommend of enabling such steps as you may recommend to be taken for the redress of any hardship from which, in your opinion, the poorer classes may suffer under the existing law and administration.
The object of this commission was twofold. In the first place it was to ascertain whether or not additional or further ground for divorce should be allowed. With that I have nothing whatever to do; it has no part or lot in my motion. The other object of the commission was to ascertain what relief could be given to the poorer classes, and it is this phase of the matter with which I wish particularly to deal. Majority and minority reports were

made by this commission, the Archbishop of York, Sir William R. Anson and Sir Lewis T. Dibdin signing the minority report. The differences of opinion between these gentlemen and the gentlemen of the majority was based exclusively on the question as to whether or not the grounds for divorce should be added to or increased. The Archbishop of York, Sir William Anson and Sir Lewis T. Dibdin dissented, making a minority report as to increasing the grounds. On the other point, the propriety of lessening the expense to the poorer classes, they were entirely in accord with the majority of the commission. So that, although both majority and minority reports were submitted, the whole commission, including the former judge of the Divorce Court and tne Archbishop of York, the Primate of England, were heartily in accord with the terms of the resolution I have moved to-night. I should like to read briefly from page 172 of the minority report the views of the Archbishop of York, which I consider to be very appropriate in this connection:
The question submitted to the present Royal Commission is, in effect, whether the statute law made by Parliament in 1857 needs reconsideration either as to the grounds of divorce, or as to courts. The nation more emphatically than in 1857 now includes persons of every variety of creed and of no creed, all of whom have a right to be considered by Parliament in any amendment of the English diyorce law, and it seems to us to follow that in framing our report we are bound to treat the question on the broad grounds of the real interests of the whole community and with reference to the actual conditions of our day. We do not therefore express an opinion as to whether the action of the legislature in 1857-
That is, in establishing the court.
-was wise or unwise, or as to whether the welfare of the nation has been promoted by the divorce statute of that year. The repeal of the existing divorce act, even if desirable, is not practicable.
The Archbishop, therefore, takes exactly the view which I take. Personally, he was opposed to divorce, but, realizing that legislation permitting divorce was in existence, and finding it practically impossible to repeal it, he took what I contend to be the sensible view, and said: Whilst I should not have approved it originally, since the Act is there and cannot be repealed, let us make it as near perfect as possible. I wish to quote again from the minority report:
With regard to the question as to whether greater facilities are necessary to enable persons of slender means living at considerable distance from London to exercise their statutory rights
under the divorce acts, it is of course absolutely incontestable that no one ought to be deprived of his legal rights merely by poverty. Further, the evidence has in our opinion established that the centralization of all divorce business in London and the cost of divorce proceedings have in fact prevented a considerable number of poor persons and persons of small means from bringing suits in the divorce court, which, but for the expense they might have brought successfully.
For any one who wishes to take the trouble to read it, there are here heartrending accounts of the effects of the law upon poorer families. The deserted husband or wife, as the case might be, being unable to marry again, the usual results, the children of course paying the penalty, came about.
I shall not further occupy the attention of the House, but will conclude by urging the Government to take this matter into their serious and speedy consideration. I desire also to urge upon the members of this House the fact that this is not a political question; it is a subject which, to my mind, should appeal to every representative of the people. We must not forget that every member of this House, no matter whence he comes, does not represent only the people who elected him, for that is not the principle of our constitution. According to our constitution, theoretically every voter in Canada comes to Ottawa to make the laws, but inasmuch as practically that is impossible, the country has been divided into constituencies, each of which is allowed to send one or more representatives to Ottawa to represent all the people of this country. Therefore, every member sitting in this House, I care not on which side of the House he sits, is a representative of the injured poor of this country who are deprived of the right of redress which their wealthier neighbours have. I plead with the Government and I plead with hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House, not only for the sake of the injured persons; not only for the sake of the unfortunate little children who pay the heaviest penalty of all, but for the sake of society in Canada, that we may give one proof at least of the fact that the members of this House are prepared to do what is right and fair and just by the people of (Canada, (irrespective of their financial position.

As a very unwilling member
of the Divorce Committee, I should like to say a word or two with regard to this resolution. It seems to me-and I think

I am a fairly impartial observer, being an unmarried man-that it is very hard to reason sensibly about this matter, because we regard marriage as a contract, and if it be a legal contract it should be dissoluble as other contracts are; and therefore really not a marriage at all; by mutual consent the parties could go their way. But of course the contract means something more than this. There are two ways, it seems, of solving the situation. One is by divorce. Up to the time of the divorce the people are married; but where there is nullification of the marriage, it is found that they have never been married at all, and the woman is declared to have been a common prostitute from the beginning. That is what nullification means, and you can put me down as against nullification. And what is divorce? Suing for the privilege of marrying again, if you please. The parties concerned are at liberty to get an order of protection or separation from the courts; simply because they want to get married again they appeal in this heartrending way to the people of this country. Therefore I say there is no justification for divorce, and put me down as against divorce. My experience on the Divorce Committee, which reminds me of what 1 would call scavenging proceedings, has been unhappy in the extreme, and I would like to be liberated therefrom, and at once, if possible. T can see no justification for the perpetuation of any such mockeries of the marriage ceremony.

I have listened with great attention to my hon. friend the hon. member for Hastings (Mr. Northrup), who, as usual, has presented his case with that ability and legal acumen which is well known to members of this House.
I would not, under ordinary circumstances, have thought it proper to address the House on this subject because it is well known that, with other members of this House, I belong to a church which does not consider divorce and remarriage as a result of divorce as permissible. You, Sir, will have noticed that when a Bill granting a divorce, comes from the Senate to this House, the members who belong to my church do not take part in the debate and do not vote. I do not care to present to the House any religious plea on this question, and I hasten to say that I do not intend to preach or to dogmatize. Certainly the Roman Catholic church, to which I have the honour to belong, is not the only one to take the stand which it 
takes; the Anglican church in this country is opposed to the consequence of divorce, namely remarriage. My hon. friend, however, has made a strong case from his point of view, and he has urged upon the Government the necessity of bringing about reform. He stated that this country was rapidly filling up with foreigners, immigrants coming from all lands, and that the time had come when equal justice should be handed to the poor as well as to the rich. I agree with my hon. friend that immigrants are pouring into this country from all parts of the *world. We are in the process of building up our young country. But may I be permitted to say that there is more than the material aspect to that process of building up Canada, there is a moral aspect to it which must not be disregarded? In my humble judgment, speaking for a large number of Canadians, I believe, of both races and of diverse creeds, we should not enlarge the facilities to grant divorces and in this respect 1 beg to radically differ with my able and genial friend from Hastings. We boast that this is a white man's country. Why not proclaim that this is also a Christian country? Should we not on a question of this nature, profit by the experience of other peoples, of other nations, not too far from our owrn borders?
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend has made an historical survey of the subject. He has expounded very ably the custom which was followed before the Reformation in the Western church and in the Eastern church; and he has explained how it came that in English Canonical Courts, divorce decrees were granted, then Jater on by Act of Parliament, and, since 1857, if I mistake not, by regular divorce courts.	May I be permitted to go
also to fundamentals and to express the views held by not only the members of my church, but by the members of various Christian churches? Sir, in the marriage ceremony no mention is made of possible divorce. Each party swears solemnly to the other, ' for better, for worse, till death do us part.' If adultery be held to dissolve marriage it would lead to relative promiscuity since either party might remarry many times. The knowledge that they are not allowed to divorce and remarry will always tend to induce husbands and wives to minimize differences which they otherwise might magnify into occasions for separation. The risk of an agreement between the two that each should allow full liberty to the other is not one of which the law can take account, but against which

public opinion may be expected to express itself very strongly. Nothing can be worse for children, for homes and for country, than the knowledge that divorce can be easily granted. Divorce-and I come back to the point which I made a moment ago that we should profit by the experience of our near-by neighbours-divorce has been most disastrous in the United States, where each concession has led to another worse concession. Now, I have said on other occasions that on political questions we were often asked to ignore what we could learn from the United States and sometimes that, on the contrary, we were asked to follow what the United States were teaching us. The example of the United States in matters of divorce is one which we should not foilow, as it is simply appalling in its consequences. Far be it from my mind to attempt to libel the American republic. I think it is Edmund Burke who once said that you could not libel a whole people. But divorce in the United States has become not only a scandal but a curse. This is admitted by all churches and by all creeds in the United States. It is agreed and it is admitted by all good law-abiding citizens. I have under my hand some statistics which were published not very long ago, in December, 1911, upon this subject. I had the census reports of the United States but I left them in my library and have here now only this clipping from the Chicago Tribune. This shows that, according to the census of the United States, there has been in that country between the years 1887 and 1906, a total of 1,045,625 divorces. During the same period 12,832,000 marriage licenses were issued. That is to say, you have to-day in the United States one divorce for each twelve. Am I not right in saying that this facility to obtain divorce decrees has become a curse with our near neighbours the Americans? So much so, that not later than the last session of Congress, Senator Ransdell, of Louisiana, introduced a Bill to prevent divorced persons from marrying again. When introducing his Bill, Senator Ransdell said that there were twice as many divorces in the United States as in- the rest of Christendom. He said that the remedy he proposed would appear very radical indeed, but that the disease was deep-seated. It had reached an acute stage and affected all classes. Let me remind my hon. friend from Hastings (Mr. Northrup) that the divorce courts of the United States are accessible to the poorer classes as well as to the rich, and with what result-one divorce out of every
twelve marriages, as I said a moment ago. Senator Ransdell gives the following figures: In 1867 there were 9,937 divorces or 27 per 100,000 of population; in 1906, forty years later, there were 72,062 divorces or 86 per 100,000 of population. That meant that there were seven times more divorces in 1906 than in 1867, or 319 per cent, and the rate has been increasing since 1906. I read in the last census report of the United States the following:
The divorce rate, like the velocity of a falling body, is constantly increasing. The enormous increase in divorce revealed by these statistics naturally raises the question: How far this increase is to be attributed to growth in population? The rate of increase in divorce is far greater than the rate of increase in population.
President Roosevelt made the following comment on the census statistics:
This is one of the most unpleasant and dangerous features of our American life: the loosening of the marital tie among the old native American families.
My hon. friend has given a list of civilized countries which have established special divorce courts after having promulgated divorce laws. Among those countries he mentioned France. I do not pretend to know much about the other countries mentioned by my hon. friend, except those which are a part of the British Empire, but I have some knowledge of what is taking pla.ce in France through the reading of books on history, economics and social questions. The number rf divorces in France is, at the present time, causing grave alarm and apprehension. As my hon. friend well knows, there is no state church in France. The Government does not pretend to be friendly even to the church, which for centuries was the dominant church in that country. The statesmen of France-many of them indifferent in matters religious, many of them free thinkers, some of them belonging to a different faith than that of the majority of the French people-these statesmen, actually, are perturbed over the consequences of the law in regard to divorce which was adopted in 1884. In France, as in England, the opinions on the question of divorce v. ere during the last century quite chaotic. Before the revolutionary period around 1789, we find that the ecclesiastical court, as in England before the Reformation, was the only one to take cognizance of matrimonial Cases, but after the revolution the question of divorce was dealt with as it was in England at the time of the Reformation. Divorce decrees were granted during the

Canon V, Marriage and Divorce.
(Passed Session IV, Journal pp. 25, 28, 1905)
No clergymen within the jurisdiction of the Church of England in Canada shall solemnize a marriage between persons, either of whom shall have been divorced from one who is living at tho time.
I am sure I will hurt the feelings of no one. body in this House when I say that not only as a Eoman Catholic but as a Canadian, I, together with many others belonging to different churches, oppose any widened facilities to our existing divorce procedure. If I had my own way I would restrict separation as it is granted in the province of Quebec; that is to say, without any faculty of remarriage.
The State is deeply concerned in this question; the state protects family life, defines and defends the authority of parents over their children, the rights of children to the care of their parents, the obligation of husband and wife towards each other. The State, therefore, has a concern of its own in the peace of the community, the welfare of the family, the rearing of healthy children and the training of them to he good citizens. In my humble judgment, divorce and remarriage as a consequence, endanger all that. We like-especially my imperialist friends, and I have many friends amongst the imperialists-we like, to cite the example of ancient Rome. Indeed, we all admire the splendours of Rome and the genius of the Romans, but we must not forget that Rome was pagan, and that in pagan Rome repudiation and divorce were rampant. We know from the most illustrious historian of Rome, Gibbon, that the decay of the Roman Empire can be traced to the laxity of its morals. Marriage, in Rome, had become a bond which could be broken with such deplorable facility that it is said this inscription was found on a tombstone: 'Conjugi piae, inclytae univirae,' which, freely translated, means:
' Remarkable fact: here lies a pious wife who had but one husband.'
It seems to me that the granting of any further facilities to obtain divorce would be to revert to pagan Rome; to revert to paganism itself. I would rather follow the teaching of my church and the teaching of the Anglican church in Canada, which is comprised in the precept of Our Lord:
' What, therefore, God hath joined together let not man put asunder.'
Speaking of old Roman Imperialism, I might be permitted to quote what John Bright said about this mania of always borrowing from old pagan Rome. Speaking at Birmingham in 1857, John Bright said:

Now, I do not think that examples taken from pagan, sanguinary Rome, are proper models for the imitation of a Christian country, nor would I limit my hopes of the greatness of England even to the long duration of eight hundred years. But what is Rome now? The great city is dead. A poet has described her as the ' lone mother of dead empires.' Her language even, is dead. Her very tombs are empty; the ashes of her most illustrious citizens are dispersed.
The Scipios' tomb contains no ashes now. Vet, am I asked, I, who am one of the legislators of a Christian country, to measure my policy hy the policy of ancient and pagan Rome!
I believe there is no permanent greatness to a nation except it he based upon morality.
In conclusion, I think that the duty of Parliament at the present hour is not to increase the facilities for obtaining divorce decrees, but the duty of Parliament, the duty of the legislators, in the best interest of Canada and her sons, is to surround with greater safeguards the sanctity of marriage. The example which has been set by the United States on this vexed question is one rather to be dreaded than imitated by a British country, nay, hy a Christian country.

It is not my intention to follow the line of argument of my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux), because I do not think the motion of the hon. member for Hastings (Mr. Northrup) raises the question of whether divorces should be granted in Canada or not.
Were I at liberty to make a law as I would like to see it made, I am rather of the opinion that I would be entirely in harmony with my hon. friend from Rouville. . I have had some experience in divorce cases, and I must say that they have always seemed repugnant to me. I believe that they are repugnant to 'every solicitor or counsel who is unfortunate enough to have anything to do with them.	I am rather inclined to
take the opinion referred to by my hon. friend from Hastings a short time ago, which was voiced by the Archbishop of York, in a report which he made to the British Parliament, while deprecating the granting of divorces, yet he was afraid that the system had obtained such a foothold in the country that it would he impossible to repeal the law.
We might as well face conditions as they are in Canada at the present time. I do not believe that it is possible to pass a law entirely abolishing the granting of divorces in Canada. I do not mean to say

that we have not the legal right to do so, but I am rather of the opinion that the Archbishop of York was voicing the sentiment in England which has a pretty strong hold in Canada to-day. Certainly, however, were I given the right to frame a law for the whole of Canada, I should not extend the well known grounds for divorce which are supposed to exist in the Senate, and which we know are carried into effect in the four provinces in which there are divorce courts. As I apprehend the matter, the real object of the hon. member for Hastings is that this Parliament should divest itself not of the right but of the fact of granting divorces and should constitute courts in the several provinces to take charge of them, the same as there are in the three Maritime provinces and in the province of British Columbia.
My hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) has quoted some statistics in order to show that in the provinces where divorces are granted, there is a greater number than there is in the rest of Canada. That is true to some extent, but when you look into the statistics, you will be surprised to see how few divorces are granted in the Maritime provinces as compared with the rest of Canada. I have before me to-night the Canada Year Book of 1912. I do not think there are any later statistics upon this question. I find in the province of New Brunswick, which lies just alongside of the State of Maine, a state in which I believe the question of granting divorces without law or reason has been carried to as great an extreme as it has been in the State of Nevada, a state in which divorces are granted simply for incompatibility of temperament, for any fanciful device which any man or woman may put forward in order to obtain a divorce-in the province of New Brunswick lying for one hundred miles along the border of the state of Maine, and in a province in which one would think that the people might to some extent be influenced toy the social conditions existing among their neighbours across the boundary line, only 115 divorces have been granted since 1868, or in 44 years an average of about 2-6 divorces per year. It is true that during the years 1908, 1909, 1910 and 1911 there were a few more than the average. In 1908, there were 5; in 1909, 6; in 1910, 5; and in 1911,
6.	In 1912 the number dropped to 4. If you take the list right up to 1868, you will find that it runs for a few years ' no divorces granted,' , then it increases 1, 2, 53
3,	4, and then it decreases back
10 p.m. to one again. In other words, the number of divorces granted during all this period of time has not increased to any appreciable extent. The increases have been no greater' than the natural increase in population. Yet this is in a province lying for a hundred miles along the boundary line of a state in which divorces are granted for any reason which two people might put forward who wanted a dissolution of the bonds of matrimony.
I do not think that these statistics will bear out the fears entertained by hon. members who are opposed to regulating the granting of these divorces to a provincial court. I am afraid that any members who entertain those fears do not realize the difference between the method of granting divorces in our courts of law and the method in the Senate of Canada. I mention the Senate, because we know that, as a matter of fact, the whole question as to whether or not a divorce shall be granted is decided in the Senate Committee, although pro forma it has to go through this House. I think my hon. friend from Hastings stated that only one case that was favourably reported upon by the Senate Committee was refused by the Senate, and only one case that was passed by the Senate was refused by this House.
I do not wish to, say anything against the hon. members of, the Senate who act as judges in these matters. When you consider what a great majority of the members of that committee are not even professional men but men drawn from the ordinary walks of life, it is somewhat wonderful that they arrive at as true a conception of the evidence as they do. No doubt a large proportion of the justice of these decisions is due to the excellent judgment of the Chairman, who has occupied that position for so many years. Those hon. gentlemen of the House of the legal profession who have taken the trouble to read the evidence taken in the divorce cases which come before the Upper House- and I personally have read nearly every case that has come up during my experience as a member of the House-will agree with me that many divorces are granted on evidence which would not be entertained for a moment in the divorce courts of the Maritime provinces or, perhaps, of the province of British Columbia. In the divorce court the hardest case to win is the undefended case, for the simple reason that it is the duty of the divorce judge to take the position of protector of the rights of the Crown. In such a case the judge al-



most intuitively takes the ground that there is collusion, and that it is his duty to see that no injustice is done.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Is there a King's Proctor in New Brunswick?

There is not, but the
judge assumes the duties of King's Proctor, and it is the duty of the judge to see that no divorce is granted except on the strongest evidence. Knowing the law to be as it is, solicitors naturally inform their clients that there is only one ground upon which they can obtain divorce, and that they must produce evidence to that effect. Nothing but absolute evidence of adultery will do in these courts, and solicitors naturally advise their clients that it is useless to proceed with the case, and that it is a costly experiment, even in the Maritime provinces. I do not believe there is a solicitor here from the provinces of New Brunswick or Nova Scotia who has not been approached by many persons every year with requests for the institution of divorce proceedings, and who has been obliged to tell them that there is no use in their putting their money in it. The principle of granting divorces is acknowledged by this Parliament and by every province of Canada to be correct.
Except in Quebec.

I do not agree with that; I say that the principle of granting of divorces is accepted in the province of Quebec, as it is in Ontario and New Brunswick. I am free to admit-and I give them credit for it-that the dominant church in the province of Quebec has set its face against divorce, and I am against it practically as much as they are. It must be admitted that all over Canada the law provides for the granting of divorce. Admitting that to be the principle of the law, I say there is no reason why this cumbersome, expensive, unfair and discriminatory method of granting divorce should be continued. Why allow the rich man or the rich woman to come to Parliament and obtain a divorce, and deny the same privilege to the poor man or the poor woman? I have never prosecuted a divorce case through the Parliament of Canada, but I have been told that it practically involves an expenditure of $1,000. In the provinces it can be done for $100 and in many cases, probably for less. If it be right to grant divorces, then I submit that it is unfair and discriminating so to provide that the rich person can take advantage of the law, and that the poor person, because he has not $1,000 to invest in it, cannot do so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend, of course, does not mean that where it is necessary to obtain witnesses in a foreign country, possibly at a great distance from the place where the proceedings are instituted, divorce can be procured in the Maritime provinces for $100. I have seen divorce cases in the province of Nova Scotia costing, I venture to say, more, than any divorce case that ever went through the Senate.

I am fully aware of that; I think I know enough about the cost of proceedings in the courts to know that you cannot send to foreign countries and get witnesses for $100. But that is not the ordinary class of witnesses usually called upon to testify in the provincial courts. The great majority of witnesses in these cases are drawn from the immediate districts in which the litigants live. I am speaking now not of extraordinary but of ordinary cases. The first divorce case I ever had anything to do with must have cost the parties at least $3,000, and they never got a decision from the judge, as he went off the bench-my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries knows the case to which I refer. The matter was brought up in another case, and finally the divorce was granted. Strange to say, it was the husband who brought the action in the first instance and the wife in the second. However, I am speaking only oi the average case, and contending that if you admit the principle of divorce you ought not to grant it to a rich man and deny it to a poor man-and that is the result of the law as it is administered in Canada to-day, excepting the lour provinces in which there are divorce courts.
I realize that this is a somewhat delicate subject. I realize that there are many members of this House who feel that because of their conscientious convictions they ought not to vote for any change in the law. I appeal to those gentlemen and ask them to place themselves in the position of the Archbishop of York, whose very important report was referred to by the hon. member for Hastings. Let hon. gentlemen make judges of themselves to-night, and placing themselves in the position of the reverend Archbishop, they will come to the conclusion that if we are going to maintain this principle, we should put the right to enjoy the operation of the law within the reach of the poorest people of the country as well as of the richest. I think the hon. member for Hastings very properly excluded from his resolution any

word or sentiment which would raise the debatable question whether divorce should be granted; he has tried to include in his motion only such provisions as affect the machinery by which divorce should be granted. He is asking this Parliament to give to the ordinary courts of the country the right to carry on in a proper manner that which I am afraid is, in many instances, being carried on by the Parliament of Canada in an improper way. I do not think we will be doing violence to the conscientious beliefs of any class of people or any religious denomination in Canada by passing the resolution which my hon. friend has proposed to-night. I am satisfied that if this resolution carries, and the members of this House, regardless ol politics, apply themselves diligently to the matter, there will be no difficulty in devising a law which will do violence to the principles of no one, and which will do greater justice to the ordinary litigant of this country than is possible under the present system of granting divorces. *

speakeroldname: Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister oi Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I rise principally for the purpose of pointing out something that appears to me to have been overlooked, or at all events not to have been clearly put forward by the hon. gentleman who moved this resolution, and with regard to which I think the hon. member who has just taken his seat-I say it with all respect-seems to be under a misapprehension. If I felt called upon to discuss the general question whether there should be a divorce law or whether this Parliament should take steps to facilitate the obtaining of divorce in this country, I think I might very fairly satisfy myself with endorsing what has been said by the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux).
My reason for rising is to point out that this motion, while it speaks, in terms, merely of the procedure under which divorces are granted, involves, for the obtaining of the amelioration of the procedure suggested by the hon. gentleman who moves it-and, if I understand him, endorsed and approved by the hon. member who has just taken his ..oat-the enactment of a substantive law creating in those provinces in which to-day there are no divorce courts, and, more than no divorce courts, no divorce laws, creating by law a right to divorce and prescribing the cause or causes which wiP entitle persons subjected to that law to divorce.
The hon. gentleman who has just sat 53i
down is, as I understand it at all events, mistaken when he says that we recognize the principle of divorce in the law of this country. I understand perfectly that in those provinces which have divorce courts and which have also a substantive law which those courts can administer and apply, prescribing the causes giving the right to divorce, the principle of divorce is recognized by the law. But in the five provinces where those conditions do not exist, not only the courts have not jurisdiction to pronounce divorces but there is no law under which anybody is entitled to a divorce; and if this Parliament confined itself to giving jurisdiction to hear divorce cases to courts in those provinces, those courts would sit with no law to apply. You cannot, to any' purpose, confide to the court the procedure -to use the word of ihe motion-by which divorces are to be obtained, until you have first made a substantive law to which that procedure is going to apply.
Wherein is the difference between the granting of divorce for specific grounds and giving to another body the right to grant the divorce on the same ground?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
