This Parliament, to use the expression of the hon. member, grants divorce on a particular ground, passes one Act for one individual, and why does it do it? Because that individual has come to it and said:	I want to be an exception to the
general law. We talk about coming to Parliament to obtain divorces and we talk about the procedure by which divorces are granted; but the whole operation is a legislative Act, and when a man comes to Parliament, on the face of his application he does not ask for a Bill to divorce anybody, but he asks for an Act for the relief of so and so; and relief from what? From an obligation that the general law imposes upon him. In those provinces where there is no divorce court there is equally no divorce law, and the general law of those provinces, I have no hesitation in saying, does not know divorce. Most assuredly in the province I come from the law does not know divorce, and it is because there is no law in force that persons, seeking it require special legislation. Let me speak of my own province-although I have no doubt I shall be borne out by lawyers from the other provinces-the man who comes here, say from the province of Quebec, and asks this Parliament for a divorce, is asking to be made an exception to the law. He comes here because, by law, he has no

right to a divorce. If by law he had a right to a divorce, it would naturally follow that that would be .a right enforceable in a court. The reason why people have to come here is not because the courts have not jurisdiction; it is because there is no law which the courts could administer if they had the amplest jurisdiction-. So what I want to point out is that this is not a motion involving a question of mere procedure; it is a motion which, in view of the speech of the hon. gentleman who introduced it, involves voting for the creation of a substantive divorce law. I understood the hon. gentleman who just sat down to say that if he were to-day in the position of being called upon to enact a substantive divorce law and had power to do it, he would be disposed to adopt such a law as the hon. member for Rou-ville (Mr. Lemieux) thinks ought to be adopted. If that is the sort of law that the hon. member would be disposed to adopt, the law had better stay precisely where it is, because, as regards the provinces which have not divorce courts, the law to-day does not recognise the principle of divorce. If there is inequality resulting from the fact that some people come here and get private legislation that makes a law for them and takes them out of the operation of the general law, it is not because the law is unequal. .Before the law in these provinces, everybody's marriage is equally indissoluble; but this Parliament, having legislative poweT, may legislate that people who, by the law of the country, are married, and united in the bonds of an indissoluble marriage, shall be unmarried; that is all.
I understood the hon. member who moved the motion to state that he thought it would be better that there should be no divorces at all than that we should have the present unequal system. I quite agree with him that it would be better that there should be no divorces at all; but when he talks of our having an unequal system, the inequality is not the result of the unequal system; it is the result of our having no system at all, and the result of a fact which we cannot alter, that Parliament, in the exercise of its power, can pass legislation for the individual if Parliament want to. Parliament might, as Parliament can pass a law, if we choose to pass it, in the most emphatic terms, declaring that there shall be no divorce to-day and notwithstanding Parliament, by special legislation, might to-morrow make an exception, just as to-day, inasmuch as the law makes 
no provision for divorce-I am speaking of the provinces where there are no divorce courts-Parliament does step in occasionally and of its own motion withdraw a man from the operation of the law.
If we should pass an affirmative law saying there shall be no divorces, Parliament could, if Parliament desired, pass an Act for an individual who came and asked for it to take him out of the operation of that law; so that it is not in our power to bring about a condition where we could limit the powers of future parliaments, and say that they shall not, if they want to, pass legislation for the relief of particular individuals in particular cases. That is what is done to-day, and if the hon. member simply desired to alter procedure, then I would understand that the effect of his motion w-ould be to ask this House to consider ithe present procedure that is adopted with regard to the passing of this particular class of Private Bills. But evidently from the way he supports his motion, he contemplates the suggestion of a remedy consisting in the transferring over of what in this Parliament is a legislative power; and by transferring it, converting it into a judicial power, over to the judges. To do that, and to put the judges into a position to exercise any power in the matter, the first thing that would have to oe done is the enactment of a law which those judges could administer. We would have to have a law to prescribe that even adultery itself is, by law, a cause for divorce. We would have to have a law enacted to create a legal right to divorce. So that our position to-day is one that, as I understand it, we cannot possibly modify in the sense of preventing Parliament from enacting particular Acts in particular cases, and we cannot give jurisdiction to judges until we make a law of general application for the judges to administer. I think one has to really face the question whether we are prepared to introduce into the law of those provinces in which divorce does not exist, 'the institution of divorce, and to make a law as to what shall be isuffi-cient cause to justify the granting of divorce. Then of course you would leave that law, as you leave any other law, to be administered by the courts. But that is the first step in getting the jurisdiction into the hands of the court. It is not a mere matter of transferring a judicial jurisdiction from this House to the courts. The power that Parliament exercises is a legislative power, and to get power into the hands of the judges you would have to

enact a law and confer upon them the judicial power to administer that law. I want to point that out so as to make it perfectly clear that those of us who feel that we ought to vote against this motion are not open to the suggestion that we are not willing to let the procedure in regard to Private Bills be improved.
Speaking for myself, while of course I do not think these Acts should be passed, believing as I do that no man should be granted a divorce, nevertheless, if these rules could be considered with a view to improving them-and their improvement from my point of view would mean with a view to reducing the probabilities of the particular Bills passing into and becoming law-if in the exercise of its legislative power, Parliament intends in the future to enact particular Bills of this kind, I for one, would be glad to see such improvement in the procedure as would ensure the making perfectly clear in each case the existence of the cause for enacting these laws. But, as I say, the proposition that is put before us involves, if the motion stands as at present, a pronouncement upon the question whether or not we should introduce into the law of those provinces which have it not, a law of divorce. I do not propose to go into any argument upon the question of the desirability of, divorce. I rose for the purpose of making clear that what is involved in this motion is not a pure question of procedure; but the question whether the time has come when it is proper to adopt a general divorce law applicable within those provinces which have no such law at the present time. I need not say that the introduction of such a law would be a very radical change in the condition which has prevailed in this country up to the present day, and I venture to suggest that we have not had put before us any such public demand for such a radical change as would justify us in adopting it.
The hon. member who made the motion spoke of certain hardships which resulted in particular cases. The very best of laws will cause hardships in particular cases, and that we cannot get away from. But what we have to look at, is whether there exists any such demand among the people of this country based upon evidence going to show that the law as it stands to-day operates in a way to deprive the people, generally, of something which it is advantageous to them, and advantageous to the State, that they should have or whether, on the other hand, we have not reason to
congratulate ourselves upon the results that have followed upon the system to which we have been able to adhere up to the present, a system under which the law knows not divorce. When one dwells on inequalities in this regard, one dwells upon an inequality that exists and will continue to exist with regard to all things that may be obtained from Parliament by special or private legislation. It always costs something to pass private legislation. Divorce Bills are private legislation. I do not know that it has been shown that they cost more than other private legislation, and I do not think it can be said that it has been demonstrated here to-night, that even if those things were in the hands of the court that the rich man would not be in a better position to meet the expenses he would have to incur there, than the poor man, nor has it been made very clear that, as a rule at all events, the expense of passing a Bill before this House is greater than the expense of obtaining a judgment before an ordinary court. For my part I am not very much concerned in that. I would be thoroughly glad to see the inequality that exists absolutely disappear. The simplest and shortest way to bring about the disappearance of the inequality is not to put the poor man in the place the rich man is in to-day, but to take the rich man and put him in the place the poor man is in to-day, and leave them both to be governed by what is the common law of the country. Give to neither of them an exceptional law for himself. I think the part of wisdom certainly is for us to adhere to the system that has served us so well up to the present. We should have at the very least an unmistakable demand a demonstration of some measure of widespread wrong resulting from that system in the past, before we seek to alter it in such a very fundamental manner as is involved in the proposal set forth in the motion before us as explained by the hon. gentleman who so eloquently and so ably put the case in support of the motion.

Mr. Speaker, coming as I do from a province Which has a divorce court of its own, I desire to say that I listened with a great deal of interest to the discussion which has taken place this evening. I was particularly interested in listening to the reply of the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) to the case as stated by the hon. member for East Hastings (Mr. Northrup), although it did appear to me that the speech of the

hon. member for Rouville was not altogether a reply to that of the hon. member for East Hastings. The hon. member for Rouville devoted his attention to an argument against the principles of divorce as a whole. The hon. member for East Hastings, on the other hand, commenced with the premise that the condition is with us, that we have divorce. While I can appreciate the argument of the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) that there is no law in some of the eastern provinces of this Dominion providing for divorce, and that if we give the machinery to them there will be no law for them to enforce, yet, at the same time, the fact remains that the condition is that any man who can afford to and who comes to this Parliament and can produce evidence of a certain state of facts, can get his divorce. It is somewhat difficult to drive into the head of a man who is applying for a divorce, and who is put to what seems an extraordinary and unnecessary expense, the difference between the fact of a court having jurisdiction and there being no law for it to enforce.
In regard to the law as it is in force in British Columbia, I would like to say that, in my opinion, it works extremely well. It has been in force since Confederation. It has not been abused. The sanctity of the marriage state is as highly regarded there as in any other part of Canada, and I think that so long as we have as good reason as we have in Canada to be proud of the Bench we need have no fears thit such a law would be abused. I can quite realize that this is a question on which members of this House should have a very serious difference of opinion. I think that, while I am in sympathy with the idea which my hon. friend from East Hastings wishes to carry into effect, the best way probably would be to have a committee of this House appointed that would go into this question of procedure and the desirability of granting a substantive divorce law so that the House can then deal with the matter in proper form and have the whole of the evidence before it. I would, therefore, beg to move in amendment the following:
That all the words after the word 'that' to the end of the question he omitted, and the following substituted therefor:
A committee of seven members to be appointed to inquire Into the existing procedure under which divorces are granted, and to report whether any and what more satisfactory procedure should be provided in such cases.

speakeroldname: Rt. Hon. R. L. BORDEN (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have listened with a great deal of interest to the somewhat

divergent views which have been expressed in regard to this question; and I may say that those who have had the privilege of being members of this House for fifteen or twenty years, are aware that this is by no means the first time that this subject has been under discussion. My hon. friend from East Hastings (Mr. Northrup) has proposed this motion:
That, in the opinion of this House, the procedure under which divorces are granted by Parliament and the consequent unreasonable expense thereof are so unsatisfactory, besides being prohibitive to the great majority of people of Canada, that the same should be taken into immediate consideration by the Government with a view to reform, during the present session.
I do not take quite the same view of the motion as that which has been entertained by my colleague the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty). It would seem to me that my hOn. friend from East Hastings has under consideration more particularly the question of procedure, and is not aiming at the enactment of a general divorce law for the whole of Canada. In so far as the procedure by which these Bills are dealt with in Parliament is concerned, it is, in the first place, almost altogether a procedure which is provided by the rules of the Senate. I have had the opportunity, of which I, have availed myself on more than one occasion, of pointing out that the procedure of the Senate in that regard might possibly be improved in a very great measure.
One difficulty which as it has seemed to me very often arises in these proceedings before the Senate Committee is the lack of adequate precaution against collusive arrangement between the parties. In Great Britain and in some of the provinces of Canada, where there is a divorce law and where divorces are granted by the courts, it is the practice either to have the intervention of an officer known as the King's Proctor or, in the absence of the King's Proctor, the judge himself performs the duties which otherwise would be discharged by that officer, and in that way the greatest possible precaution is taken against collusive arrangement. It is also true that there are certain expenses which have to be met by persons who apply to this Parliament for a divorce that would not have to be met if they proceeded in court. It is also true that whether the divorce is applied for by means of a Private Bill in Parliament, or by ordinary judicial procedure where courts have been established

for that purpose, very great expense is sometimes involved.
It would not do for us to be under the impression that the mere enactment of a divorce law, or the establishment of courts in the various provinces of Canada, would altogether remove, in a great many cases, the inequality to which my hon. friend has alluded. The hon. member for Carle-ton, N.B., (Mr. Carvell) pointed out that in his own province, and within his own experience, there had been divorce proceedings which had cost the person who had instituted them many thousands of dollars, and that after all that great expense the proceedings had proved ineffective. Members of the bar in those provinces of Canada which have divorce courts, will realize that this is not an over-statement of the situation. There may be of course, cases in these provinces where the witnesses are readily accessible and the case is very plain, in which the expenditure necessary for the purpose of obtaining relief would be very light. At the same time, the expense of proceedings of that kind in the Senate, where witnesses are readily available and where large expenditure for the purpose of bringing them from a foreign country is not necessary, would also be relatively light, except for the cost of advertisement; the exact necessity for which I am unable to appreciate, and in that respect I am very much of the opinion which was expressed by my hon. friend (Mr. Northrup).
One difficulty which has been alluded to, and it is by no means undeserving of consideration, is the fact that members, whether of the Senate or the Commons, sometimes are not liable to realize to the full that in dealing with these cases they are supposed to be acting in a strictly judicial capacity, and to render their judgment strictly upon the evidence which has been adduced.
However, the whole situation, as to divorce in the five provinces is this: that while there is not any general law in these provinces which enables persons who consider themselves entitled to divorce to obtain it, there has been ever since 1867 in this Parliament the virtual constitution of a court which does deal with divorce cases from these provinces. It is equally true that not only the Senate but the House of Commons consider themselves bound in dealing with this question to proceed upon certain well-defined principles which regulate the granting of divorce in the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. In fact, rule
152 of the Senate makes this absolutely plain:
152. In cases not provided for by these rulesr the general principles upon which the Imperial Parliament proceeds in dissolving marriage, and the rules, usages, and forms of the House of Lords in respect of divorce proceedings may, so far as they are applicable, be applied to divorce proceedings before the Senate and before the standing committee on divorce.
The result seems to be that although there is no divorce law, and no divorce tribunal established in the five provinces, Parliament has nevertheless in a certain sense constituted itself into a tribunal for that purpose, and it is to that tribunal that persons desiring this relief come by the procedure of a private Bill.
I am not at all disposed to say that the procedure in the Senate could not be improved. In fact I have expressed the opinion on more than one occasion that it might. It might perhaps be improved by greater safeguards in respect to undefended cases, although I concur absolutely in what has been said as to the very excellent work which has been performed by Senator Kirchhoffer during the many years he has been Chairman of the Senate Committee on Divorce. Possibly some of the useless expense might be done away with to the end that the inequality which has been aliuded to by the hon. member (Mr. Northrup) might to a certain extent be relieved in so far as that expense does not provide any safeguards such as are provided in the courts of the land which deal with divorce cases.
I venture to think that the motion proposed by my hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Barnard) would be a more direct and effective way of ascertaining whether or not the procedure can be improved, than the motion proposed by my hon. friend from Hastings (Mr. Northrup). It must, of course, be realized by hon. members of this. House that so long as the practice which has prevailed for so many years, of instituting these proceedings in the Senate, is followed in the future, the rules of the Senate will be the controlling factor in the situation, and therefore, a motion such as that of my hon. friend from Victoria would probably be more effective if it made provision for an inquiry into this subject by a joint committee of this House and of the Senate. It wou.d seem to me that it might be well for us, before proceeding further with the discussion of the subject, to have that consideration in mind. Possibly some in-

quiry might be made of the members of the Upper House as to whether or not a joint committee, such as I have suggested, could not be appointed before the end of the session. In that view I would not protract the discussion further, and I therefore move that the debate be adjourned.

I am afraid
that in rising to speak on this motion I may go against the rule which was adopted last year when introducing the closure; but perhaps as the subject we are discussing now is not of such a contentious nature as that which we had before us last year, I may be allowed the privilege of saying a few words upon the motion of my right hon.' friend. If I have correctly comprehended the whole tenor of the discussion, from the speech of my hon. friend from Hastings (Mr. Northrup) down to the speech of the Prime Minister, there is no disposition to favour the idea of introducing a divorce law, because every hon. gentleman who has spoken in support of the idea of my hon. friend (Mr. Northrup) has stated that it is not the intention to further extend the principles upon which divorces are at the present time granted.
My hon. friend, if I apprehend him correctly, rather puts himself behind the minority report of the commission which sat upon the subject some two years ago in England, which minority report said that while they would not favour initiating an improvement of procedure, they would favour an improvement of procedure. This is the spirit in which my hon. friend has approached the subject. I have only this to say to him that, whilst he deprecates the idea of divorce, if his motion means anything at all, it has for its object to make more easy the granting of divorces by this Parliament. In other words, he thinks that divorce is an evil, but he says:	The evil
exists; we find it here; every year by law we grant this evil one more application; but still by his motion he desires to make it more easy to make applications for divorce and to grant more than we do at present. That does not seem to me to be a logical position at all.
For my part, I rather agree with the statement made by my hon. friend the Minister of Justice that up to this time the law does not know divorce, and that we had better stand by that position. We are in this position in Canada to-day, that there are fewer divorces in this country than in perhaps any other civilized country in the world. It is true that there may be an in-

justice done to somebody by the procedure that we have at the present time. There is no law that we can make, of any exceptional nature at all,- which will not work some injustice upon some individual. On the whole, however, such laws are for the benefit of the State, and I believe that it is for the benefit of the State that we have no divorce law.
The position taken by my hon. friend from Hastings is that we have no law, but ,we have a practice. The practice is such jthat it may work injuriously to certain parties and therefore he says that we should make this practice more easy and more accessible to those who have not the benefit of it to-day. This is simply providing for the extension of a thing which is acknowledged to be an evil. The reasoning upon this point of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice seems to be conclusive, and for my part I entirely agree with him.
There is just one point raised by my hon. friend the Minister of Justice on which I am not disposed to agree with him at the moment, but, whether I agree or not, it is merely a matter of speculation. My hon. friend has stated that we have divorce courts in four provinces, and that in the other five provinces we have no divorce court and we have no law. He is quite right that we have no divorce law in the province of Quebec, but I am not quite sure that there is not a divorce law in the province of Ontario. From my reading of the history of the case, I think that a divorce law such as it was then in England was introduced into the province of Upper Canada when it was created in 1791. The English laws were introduced into Upper Canada at that time. There was a divorce law in England at that time, and I think that it is in existence to-day in the province of Ontario. It is, however, a dormant law, whether it was effective or not, and the province of Ontario cannot bring it into force even if it is in existence, because by the Confederation Act the province has been deprived of the privilege of legislating in regard to divorces. Therefore, even if the law exists in Ontario, it is purely in an academic way; the province of Ontario cannot grant divorces, and it must be by this Parliament and this Parliament alone that such divorces are granted. I bring this matter to the attention of my hon. friend merely as a matter of speculation. On the other points which he has brought up, I repeat that I entirely agree with the views of my hon. friend the

Minister of Justice. I believe that we had better remain where we have been for the last forty years in this Confederation, and that the Canadian law should continue to ignore divorce as it has done heretofore. [DOT]
Motion of Mr. Borden agreed to, and debate adjourned.
On motion of Mr. Borden, the House adjourned at 11 p.m.
Tuesday, February 17, 1914.
